title: Retrieval-augmented generation
summary: How an app finds the right passages from its own documents and gives them to a language model, so answers come from your data instead of the model's memory.

blocks.p: A language model knows what was in its training data, up to a cutoff date. It doesn't know your refund policy, your internal wiki, or yesterday's price change. Asked anyway, it may write a fluent answer that is wrong.
Retraining the model on your documents is slow and expensive, and has to happen again whenever they change. Pasting every document into every prompt is too long and too costly.
**Retrieval-augmented generation** (RAG) looks up the passages that matter for each question and puts them in the prompt. The model answers from those passages.

list: **Split** each document into **chunks** of a few hundred tokens, often with a little overlap so a sentence isn't cut from its context.
**Embed** each chunk into a vector, as in the vector search lesson.
**Store** the vectors with the chunk text and its source, such as the document title and link.
**Embed the question** with the same model.
**Retrieve** the nearest chunks, often the top 5 to 20.
**Generate**: send the model the question, the chunks and instructions to answer only from them and cite the sources.

blocks.caption: Indexing runs ahead of time. At question time the app retrieves the nearest chunks and sends them with the question. Without retrieval the model can only guess.

blocks.p: Most bad answers come from retrieval, not generation. If the right chunk isn't retrieved, the model can't use it. So test retrieval on its own: for a set of questions, check whether the chunk with the answer comes back.

list: **Chunks lose context.** A chunk saying "the limit is 30 days" doesn't say what the limit is for. Add the document title or a short summary to each chunk before embedding.
**Vectors miss exact terms.** Product codes and names are better matched by keyword search such as BM25. Run both and merge the ranked lists with a method like Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
**The first results aren't the best.** A **reranker**, usually a cross-encoder that reads each question and chunk together, can reorder a larger set and keep the best few.
**Permissions and updates lag.** Filter results by the caller's access rights before sending chunks to the model, and delete stale chunks when source documents change.
**More context isn't always better.** Models can miss facts placed in the middle of a long prompt. Send fewer, better chunks.

blocks.caption: Tokens sent with each question, and the input cost of a million questions at a given price.

list: **The name comes from a 2020 paper.** Lewis and others introduced RAG in [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401).

**Context helps retrieval.** Anthropic's [Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/research/contextual-retrieval) adds a short, chunk-specific context before embedding, and combines it with keyword search and reranking.

**Position in the prompt matters.** [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) found that models often used information at the start or end of a long input better than information in the middle.
**Show the sources.** Return the documents each answer used, so users can check it, and so you can see which chunks led to a wrong answer.
RAG retrieves the passages relevant to a question and gives them to the model with it.
Indexing splits documents into chunks, embeds them and stores them with their source.
Most failures are retrieval failures, so measure retrieval on its own.
Add context to chunks, combine keyword and vector search, rerank, and send fewer, better chunks.
